title: Jon Yablonski, Laws of UX: Fitts's Law
text:
## Fitts's Law

The time to acquire a target is a function of the distance to and size of the target.

## What it means for interface design

Movement time to a target depends inversely on the target size and increases with the distance to it. In practice a larger, closer target is faster and more accurate to hit than a smaller, farther one. There is a speed to accuracy tradeoff: faster movements and smaller targets produce higher error rates.

## Takeaways

Touch targets should be large enough that users can accurately select them. Provide adequate spacing between touch targets so they are not accidentally hit. Place targets in areas of the interface that allow them to be easily and quickly acquired, for example near the current point of user focus.

## Origin

The psychologist Paul Fitts studied human motor control in 1954. His research demonstrated that the time required to move to a target is a function of the distance to and size of the target. This principle shaped modern UI conventions such as making interactive buttons larger on mobile devices, since smaller buttons take more time and effort to select accurately, and reducing the distance between a user's area of focus and the related action.

title: Jon Yablonski, Laws of UX: Hick's Law
text:
## Hick's Law

The time it takes to make a decision increases with the number and complexity of choices.

## What it means for interface design

When response speed matters, minimize choices to reduce decision time. Every additional option a user must interpret and evaluate adds to the time and cognitive effort of choosing.

## Takeaways

Reduce the number of choices when response time is critical to decrease decision time. Break complex tasks into smaller steps to decrease cognitive load. Avoid overwhelming users by highlighting recommended options. Use progressive onboarding to minimize cognitive load for new users. Be careful not to simplify to the point of abstraction, where meaning is lost.

## Origin

Hick's Law is named after British psychologist William Edmund Hick and American psychologist Ray Hyman. In 1952 the pair examined the relationship between the number of stimuli present and an individual's reaction time to any given stimulus. They found that increasing the number of choices increases decision time logarithmically, because users must spend effort interpreting and deciding among them.

title: Jon Yablonski, Laws of UX: Jakob's Law
text:
## Jakob's Law

Users spend most of their time on other sites. This means that users prefer your site to work the same way as all the other sites they already know.

## What it means for interface design

Design consistency with established conventions lets users leverage existing mental models. A mental model is a compressed model based on what we think we know about a system and how it works. When your interface matches the patterns users already understand from other products, they can focus on their task instead of learning how your interface works.

## Takeaways

Users transfer expectations they have built around one familiar product onto another that appears similar. By leveraging existing mental models you create superior user experiences in which users can focus on their tasks rather than on learning new models. When making changes, minimize discord by letting users continue using a familiar version for a limited time.

## Origin and example

Jakob's Law is named after Jakob Nielsen, co-founder of the Nielsen Norman Group, who pioneered discount usability engineering and invented several usability methods including heuristic evaluation. YouTube's 2017 redesign demonstrated the principle by letting desktop users preview the new Material Design interface, offer feedback, and revert to the old version if they chose, reducing the friction of transition.

title: Jon Yablonski, Laws of UX: Miller's Law
text:
## Miller's Law

The average person can only keep 7 (plus or minus 2) items in their working memory.

## What it means for interface design

Miller's Law is frequently misapplied. Do not use the magical number seven to justify unnecessary design limitations such as capping a navigation menu at seven items. The more useful lesson is to organize content into smaller, meaningful chunks so users can process, understand, and remember it more easily.

## Takeaways

Do not use the magical number seven to justify unnecessary design limitations. Organize content into smaller chunks to help users process, understand, and memorize easily. Remember that short term memory capacity will vary per individual, based on their prior knowledge and situational context.

## Origin and related concepts

In 1956 the psychologist George Miller asserted that the span of immediate memory and absolute judgment were both limited to around seven pieces of information. He introduced the term bit as the basic unit of information, the amount needed to make a decision between two equally likely alternatives, and the concept of channel capacity, the threshold up to which a person can reliably distinguish information before confusion sets in. Miller's Law connects to chunking (grouping information into meaningful units), cognitive load, and choice overload.

title: Jon Yablonski, Laws of UX: Aesthetic-Usability Effect
text:
## Aesthetic-Usability Effect

Users often perceive aesthetically pleasing design as design that's more usable.

## What it means for interface design

An attractive interface generates a positive emotional response that leads users to believe the product works better than it actually does. This means visual polish is not merely decorative: it directly shapes perceived usability and how forgiving users are of small problems.

## Takeaways

An aesthetically pleasing design creates a positive response in people's brains and leads them to believe the design actually works better. People are more tolerant of minor usability issues when the design of a product or service is aesthetically pleasing. Visually pleasing design can mask usability problems and prevent issues from being discovered during usability testing, so aesthetics can hide real defects.

## Origin

Researchers Masaaki Kurosu and Kaori Kashimura of the Hitachi Design Center conducted the foundational study in 1995. They tested 26 variations of an ATM interface with 252 participants, asking them to rate each design on ease of use and on aesthetic appeal. They found a stronger correlation between the participants' ratings of aesthetic appeal and perceived ease of use than between aesthetic appeal and actual ease of use. Interface aesthetics measurably influence user perception even when people consciously try to judge the underlying function.

title: Jon Yablonski, Laws of UX: Doherty Threshold
text:
## Doherty Threshold

Productivity soars when a computer and its users interact at a pace (less than 400ms) that ensures that neither has to wait on the other.

## What it means for interface design

System feedback that arrives faster than 400 milliseconds keeps users engaged and productive, because attention is not lost waiting on the machine. When true response cannot be that fast, perceived performance techniques close the gap.

## Takeaways

Provide system feedback within 400ms in order to keep users' attention and increase productivity. Use perceived performance to improve response time and reduce the perception of waiting. Animation is one way to visually engage people while loading or processing is happening in the background. Progress bars help make wait times tolerable, regardless of their accuracy. Purposefully adding a delay to a process can actually increase its perceived value and instill a sense of trust, even when the process itself takes less time.

## Origin

Walter J. Doherty and Arvind J. Thadani published the 400 millisecond threshold in the IBM Systems Journal in 1982. Their research replaced the prior 2 second standard: when systems responded within 400ms, usage became habitual, almost addictive. The threshold builds on earlier work by Robert B. Miller on man computer conversational response times and Brad A. Myers on progress indicators.

title: Brad Frost, Atomic Design (Chapter 2: Atomic Design Methodology)
text:
## Atomic Design

Atomic design is a methodology for creating design systems, composed of five distinct stages working together to create interface design systems in a more deliberate and hierarchical manner. The five stages are atoms, molecules, organisms, templates, and pages. The stages borrow from chemistry: atoms combine into molecules, which combine into more complex organisms.

## Atoms

Atoms are the basic building blocks of matter, and in interfaces they are the foundational building blocks that cannot be broken down further without ceasing to function. They include basic HTML elements like form labels, inputs, buttons, and other elements that cannot be broken down without ceasing to be useful. Atoms have their own unique properties such as a color palette, typography, and hidden qualities like animations, and they serve as a reference that helps maintain consistency.

## Molecules

Molecules are relatively simple groups of UI elements functioning together as a unit. For example a form label, search input, and button atom can join to form a search form molecule. Frost writes that molecules are groups of atoms bonded together that take on distinct new properties. Building up from atoms to molecules encourages a do one thing and do it well mentality.

## Organisms

Organisms are relatively complex UI components composed of groups of molecules, atoms, and/or other organisms, forming distinct sections of an interface. A header organism might contain a logo atom, a primary navigation molecule, and a search form molecule. Organisms can consist of similar or different molecule types, for example a product grid organism made of repeated product molecules.

## Templates

Templates are page level objects that place components into a layout and articulate the design's underlying content structure. Templates focus on the page's underlying content structure rather than the final content. They demonstrate how the components look and function together and provide the guardrails for the dynamic content that will fill them.

## Pages

Pages are specific instances of templates that show what a UI looks like with real representative content in place. Pages are where the design system's effectiveness is tested, because real content reveals whether the templates hold up. Pages also help articulate variations in templates, for example an article with a very long headline versus a very short one.

## Key principle

Atomic design is not a linear process where you finish atoms then move to molecules and so on. Rather it is a mental model that allows us to concurrently create final UIs and their underlying design systems. The stages let designers and developers move back and forth between the abstract building blocks and the concrete final interface.

title: W3C, WCAG 2.1 Understanding SC 2.5.5 Target Size (Enhanced)
text:
## Success Criterion 2.5.5 Target Size (Enhanced)

The size of the target for pointer inputs is at least 44 by 44 CSS pixels, except in the following cases.

## The four exceptions

Equivalent: the target is available through an equivalent link or control on the same page that is at least 44 by 44 CSS pixels. Inline: the target is in a sentence or block of text. User agent control: the size of the target is determined by the user agent and is not modified by the author. Essential: a particular presentation of the target is essential to the information being conveyed.

## Intent

The intent is to help users who may have trouble activating a small target because of hand tremors, limited dexterity, or other reasons. Touch is particularly affected because fingers are less precise than a mouse pointer and can obscure the target. Small targets that are close together lead to accidental activation of the wrong control. The success criterion recommends larger targets especially when the control is used frequently, the result is hard to undo, the target is hard to reach, or it is part of a sequential task.

## Who benefits

Users with mobility impairments such as hand tremors, users with large fingers or operating a device one handed, users in a moving vehicle subject to environmental vibration, users with low vision who benefit from larger hit areas, and users on touchscreen mobile devices.

title: Katie Sherwin, Nielsen Norman Group: Placeholders in Form Fields Are Harmful
text:
## Placeholders in Form Fields Are Harmful

Using placeholder text inside a form field as a substitute for a visible label undermines usability. It looks clean and reduces clutter, but it creates significant problems because the hint disappears the moment the user starts typing.

## The usability problems

Disappearing text strains short term memory: once the placeholder vanishes on focus, users can forget what the field was for, especially in long or multi step forms. Users cannot check their work: with no persistent label they cannot verify what they entered before submitting, or catch autocomplete errors. Error recovery is hard: if validation fails, users must clear a field to see the hint again. Keyboard and screen reader users are penalized: people tabbing quickly do not pause to read a disappearing hint, and screen reader support for placeholders is unreliable. Empty fields draw the eye, so completed fields with placeholder like values become hard to scan. Users may mistake placeholder text for a pre filled default value and skip the field entirely. Some placeholders require manual deletion before typing.

## Accessibility concerns

Default gray placeholder text usually fails color contrast requirements. Placeholder as label increases cognitive load for users with motor or cognitive impairments, and screen readers do not reliably announce placeholder content.

## Recommendation

Use clear, visible labels placed outside and above empty form fields so they persist while the user types. If you need supplementary hints or format examples, place that help text outside the field as well, where it stays visible.

title: GOV.UK Design System, Error message component
text:
## Error message component

Use the error message component with the validation pattern to tell the user what has gone wrong and how to fix it. Show an error message next to the field, in red, and repeat it in the error summary at the top of the page.

## Placement

Place the error message in red after the question text and any hint text, and before the input. Give the input a red border to connect the message visually to the field. Never clear the fields the user has already filled in when you show an error.

## How to write an error message

Be clear and concise. Say what happened and what to do about it. Do not use technical jargon like form post error or error 0x0000000643. Do not use negative words like forbidden, illegal, or you forgot. Do not use please (it implies a choice), do not say sorry, and avoid the words valid and invalid. Do not use humour such as oops.

## Match the label and be specific

Use the same wording in the error message as in the question label. For the label How many hours do you work a week? the error is Enter how many hours you work a week. Avoid generic messages like An error occurred, Answer the question, or Fill in the field. Target the specific problem, whether the field was empty, too long, or in the wrong format.

## Consistency and accessibility

Use identical wording next to the field and in the error summary component. Include a visually hidden Error: prefix before the message so screen reader users hear, for example, Error: The date your passport was issued must be in the past.

title: Therese Fessenden, Nielsen Norman Group: Modal & Nonmodal Dialogs
text:
## Modal and nonmodal dialogs

A modal dialog appears on top of the main content and moves the system into a special mode requiring user interaction. It disables the background content until the user explicitly addresses it. A nonmodal dialog does not restrict interaction with the rest of the page: users can continue their current task, move or minimize the dialog, or ignore it if it is not relevant.

## Why modals are costly

Modal dialogs interrupt the user's workflow and force attention away from the current task, creating a cognitive recovery burden. They block context by hiding the background information the user may need to respond. They demand immediate attention and prevent task continuation. They add interaction cost, since users must take an extra step to dismiss them.

## When a modal is appropriate

Use modal dialogs for critical error warnings and irreversible actions, for essential information the user needs to continue, for breaking a complex workflow into digestible steps (with a progress indicator), for information that significantly reduces user effort, and for high stakes preventive messages.

## Anti-pattern: modal overuse

Do not use modal dialogs for newsletter signups or other nonessential information, mid checkout interruptions, complex decisions that require external information, or upsells and persuasion. Overusing modals produces a Boy Who Cried Wolf effect: users learn to dismiss them reflexively and stop trusting them, so they ignore the modals that actually matter.

title: Samhita Tankala, Nielsen Norman Group: Skeleton Screens 101
text:
## Skeleton Screens 101

A skeleton screen is a design pattern used to indicate that a page is loading while providing users with a wireframe like visual that mimics the layout of the page. It applies to full page loads and gives users a preview of where content will appear, creating the illusion that the page is gradually transitioning into its final format.

## Three types

Static content and image skeleton screens are the most common: gray boxes stand in for content and images matching the final page structure. Animated skeleton screens add pulsating movement, gradients, or fading to maintain engagement. Frame display skeleton screens show only header, footer, and background, and are not recommended.

## When to use which loading indicator

For loads under 1 second, no indicator is needed. For loads of about 2 to 10 seconds, use skeleton screens or spinners. For loads over 10 seconds, use a progress bar so users can see how much longer they will wait. Skeleton screens are better than spinners when the full screen is loading, because the wireframe gives users a sense of what the page will look like.

## Benefits and caution

Skeleton screens reduce the chance that users abandon a page that looks broken, and lower cognitive load by establishing a mental model of the layout before content arrives. One caution: animated skeleton screens can create accessibility issues for some users, for example those sensitive to motion.

title: GOV.UK Design System, Button component
text:
## Button component

Use buttons to help users carry out an action like starting an application or saving their information. Write button text in sentence case that describes the action, using a verb: Start now, Sign in, Continue, Save and continue, Add another, Pay, Sign out.

## Button types

The default button is the primary call to action. Avoid using multiple default buttons on a single page, because too many calls to action make it hard for users to know what to do next. Start buttons are green and mark the entry point to a service; they usually do not submit form data, so use a link styled as a start button. Research showed that using green for start buttons improved click through rates. Secondary buttons are for secondary actions. Warning buttons are red and reserved for actions with serious, destructive consequences that cannot be easily undone, such as permanently deleting an account. Do not rely on the red colour alone to communicate the seriousness; make the action and its consequence clear in words too. Inverse (white) buttons are for dark backgrounds and must keep a contrast ratio of at least 4.5:1.

## Placement

Align the primary action button to the left edge of your form.

## Disabled buttons anti-pattern

Disabled buttons have poor contrast and can confuse some users, so avoid them if possible. Only disable a button if research shows it makes the interface easier to understand. As an alternative to disabling the submit button, let users submit and then show clear validation errors.

## Preventing double clicks

To reduce accidental duplicate submissions, you can set data-prevent-double-click to true on submit buttons, but still protect against duplicates on the server.

title: Aurora Harley, Nielsen Norman Group: Icon Usability
text:
## Icon Usability

Truly universal icons are rare. Very few icons are universally recognized: the main examples are the house for home, the printer for print, and the magnifying glass for search. Most icons remain ambiguous to users because the same symbol is associated with different meanings across different interfaces, and even a slight difference in meaning or functionality hinders a user's ability to understand and rely on an icon.

## The ambiguity problem

Icons such as the hamburger menu, the heart, and the star are used inconsistently across products for different functions, so users cannot reliably predict what they do. An icon that is unclear forces users to guess, or to click to find out, which raises interaction cost.

## Always pair icons with text labels

The strongest recommendation is that icons should have a visible text label at all times, without requiring any interaction from the user. Relying on hover to reveal a label increases interaction cost and fails entirely on touch devices. A clear text label removes ambiguity and makes the feature discoverable.

## Mystery-meat navigation danger

Ambiguous, unlabeled icons create features users never find. In testing, a clock icon meant to represent browsing history was recognized by no participants, so the feature went unused. This is the mystery meat problem: when a control's meaning is hidden behind an unlabeled symbol, users cannot discover it.

## Design best practices

Keep icons simple and schematic rather than adding realistic detail. If it takes more than about five seconds to think of an effective icon for a concept, that concept probably cannot be communicated by an icon alone. Test icons for recognizability and memorability with real users, and consider platform standard and competitor conventions.

title: Kara Pernice, Nielsen Norman Group: Designing Effective Carousels
text:
## Carousel usability problems

Carousels (rotating banners of large images) are frequently overlooked. People often immediately scroll past these large images and miss the content, especially any frame after the first one, on both desktop and mobile. Because a person often sees only one image, a single slide can give the wrong idea about an organization. Auto advancing content that looks like an advertisement triggers banner blindness: eyetracking research found that animated ads get looked at only 27% of the time.

## Auto-forwarding vs manual control

Do not auto forward if you are uncertain about the right timing, because content that moves too fast or too slow frustrates users, or if the content resembles an ad, or on mobile where auto rotation slows the page and users scroll below the carousel before the frame changes. If you do time transitions, use roughly 3 words per second as a reading speed baseline.

## Best practices if you must use one

Limit the carousel to about 5 or fewer frames so users can recognize and engage with them. Use crisp, legible text and images aligned with the organization's mission. Show a progress indicator with the frame count and current position. Use recognizable navigation controls and avoid tiny dots on mobile. Place the controls inside the carousel, not below or past the fold. Make each frame's control distinctive and representative. Size buttons and links large enough to see and click. Most important, place any content that matters somewhere else in the UI as well, because carousel visibility is unreliable.

title: W3C, WCAG 2.1 Understanding SC 2.4.7 Focus Visible
text:
## Success Criterion 2.4.7 Focus Visible

Any keyboard operable user interface has a mode of operation where the keyboard focus indicator is visible.

## Intent

The purpose is to help users know which element among multiple has the keyboard focus at any point in time. A sighted keyboard user needs to see the focus indicator to operate the page. The phrase mode of operation allows a user agent to optimize when the indicator is shown, but authors must ensure there is at least one mode where the keyboard focus indicator stays visible and is not time limited.

## Why it matters

Without a visible focus indicator, sighted keyboard users cannot tell where they are on the page and cannot effectively operate the interface. Users with attention limitations, short term memory limitations, or executive function difficulties also benefit from being able to locate the current point of focus.

## Examples

A text field shows a blinking cursor or highlights its text when focused. An interactive control such as a button or link shows a visible border or outline when it receives keyboard focus.

## Relationship to focus order

Focus Visible complements SC 2.4.3 Focus Order, which requires that components receive focus in an order that preserves meaning and operability. Together they ensure keyboard navigation is both logically ordered and visually perceivable.

title: Tim Neusesser, Nielsen Norman Group: Infinite Scrolling, When to Use It and When to Avoid It
text:
## Infinite scrolling: when to use, when to avoid

Infinite scrolling loads more content automatically as the user reaches the bottom of the page, with no pagination. It works well for open ended content consumption without a specific goal, such as social media, entertainment, and news feeds, where it reduces interruptions, creates a seamless experience, lowers interaction cost, and suits mobile devices where users already scroll.

## When infinite scroll fails

Infinite scroll is a poor fit for goal oriented tasks. Refinding content is hard: users lack landmarks, and when they use the back button they often return to the top of the page rather than their previous position, forcing them to re scroll through everything they already saw. Footer access is broken: the constant stream of new content prevents users from reaching useful information usually kept in the footer, such as contact details and return policies. It is problematic when users need to find something specific, compare items in a long list, or inspect only a few items at the top. It also creates an illusion of completeness, causes accessibility challenges for keyboard and screen reader users, increases page load time, and can harm SEO.

## Recommended alternatives

For goal oriented tasks use pagination or a Load More button instead of pure infinite scroll. A Load More button is a middle ground: it lets users control when more content loads while keeping the footer reachable.

title: W3C Design Tokens Community Group, Design Tokens Format Module
text:
## What is a design token

A design token is information associated with a human readable name, at minimum a name and value pair. Tokens are a platform agnostic way to express design decisions such as color, spacing, typography, and duration, so those decisions can be shared across different disciplines, tools, and technologies. They establish a common vocabulary across an organization and act as a single source of truth, in contrast to hard coding the same raw value in many places.

## Structure of a token

Every token has a name, a case sensitive string that uniquely identifies it within its group, and a value accessed through the $value property, which holds the actual design decision. A token may also carry optional metadata: $type categorizes the token (for example color, dimension, duration) so tools know how to interpret the value; $description explains the token's purpose and intended usage; $extensions holds vendor or tool specific data; and $deprecated marks a token that is no longer recommended.

## Aliases and references

A token's value can reference another token's value instead of repeating a raw value. These aliases (also called references) let you build semantic tokens on top of core tokens, for example color.action.primary referencing color.blue.600. This removes repetition, encodes intent, and keeps the system consistent because updating the referenced token updates everything that points to it.

title: Alita Kendrick, Nielsen Norman Group: Microinteractions in User Experience
text:
## Microinteractions in user experience

A microinteraction is a trigger feedback pair in which the trigger can be a user action or an alteration in the system's state, and the feedback is a narrowly targeted response to the trigger, communicated through small, highly contextual, usually visual changes in the user interface. The concept and a model for designing microinteractions come from Dan Saffer's 2014 book Microinteractions.

## The role of feedback

Microinteractions provide feedback to the user, often by conveying system status or helping users prevent errors. Good feedback confirms that an action registered, communicates what the system is doing, and guides the user toward the correct next step, all without pulling attention away from the main task.

## Examples

A pulsating heart animation on a product shows that it was favorited. A pull to refresh gesture shows a circular progress indicator that communicates the system is working. A dynamic password requirements list updates as the user types, preventing errors before submission. An app icon that shakes signals the system is waiting for further input.

## Why they matter

Microinteractions improve the experience by encouraging engagement, displaying system status, preventing errors, and expressing brand identity. Executed well, these small moments differentiate a product from competitors that ignore them.

title: Luke Wroblewski, Touch Target Sizes
text:
## Touch target sizes

Touch targets need to be large enough to hit accurately, because a finger is far less precise than a mouse pointer. Luke Wroblewski compiles the recommendations from major platform makers and from ergonomics research.

## Platform recommendations

Apple recommends a minimum target size of 44 pixels wide by 44 pixels tall (later expressed as 44 points on Retina displays). Microsoft recommends a preferred touch target size of 9mm (about 34px), a minimum touch target size of 7mm (about 26px), and a minimum spacing between elements of 2mm (about 8px). Microsoft advises enlarging targets when the element is touched frequently, when a touch error has severe consequences, when the element sits at a screen edge, or when it is part of a sequential task. Nokia recommends that a touchable element be no smaller than 1cm by 1cm (about 0.4 inch) with roughly 7mm by 7mm for an index finger and 8mm by 8mm for a thumb, with 1 to 2mm gaps and about 5mm minimum line spacing in lists.

## Research basis

The MIT Touch Lab found that the average human finger pad is 10 to 14mm and the average fingertip is 8 to 10mm. A 2005 study recommended target sizes of at least 9.2mm for single target tasks and 9.6mm for multi target tasks. The consistent lesson is that a physical target of roughly 9 to 10mm (about 44 to 48 px depending on density) balances speed and error rate, and that adequate spacing between targets is as important as size.

title: GOV.UK Design System, Table component
text:
## Table component

Use the table component to let users compare information in rows and columns. Do not use a table to lay out content on a page; use the grid system for layout instead.

## Structure and headers

Give every table a caption that acts as a descriptive heading, because a caption helps users find, navigate, and understand tables. Use column headers with scope set to col to identify what each column contains, and row headers with scope set to row to label each row. The scope attribute is what lets assistive technology tell row headers and column headers apart.

## Aligning numbers

When comparing columns of numbers, align the numbers to the right in table cells, using the numeric cell and numeric header classes. Right alignment lines up digits by place value so users can scan and compare magnitudes accurately. Tabular (monospaced) figures reinforce this because each digit occupies the same width.

## Large datasets and accessibility

For tables with a lot of data, apply the small text until tablet class to reduce text size on small screens and keep the table readable without breaking its structure. Semantic HTML with proper scope attributes ensures screen readers can communicate the relationships between headers and cells.

title: W3C, WCAG 2.1 Understanding SC 1.4.3 Contrast (Minimum)
text:
## Success Criterion 1.4.3 Contrast (Minimum)

The visual presentation of text and images of text has a contrast ratio of at least 4.5:1, except for large text, incidental text, and logotypes.

## The ratios

Normal text must have a contrast ratio of at least 4.5:1 against its background. Large text must have a contrast ratio of at least 3:1. Large text is defined as at least 18 point, or 14 point bold, or the equivalent size for Chinese, Japanese, and Korean fonts. In CSS pixels this is roughly 24px, or about 18.66px when bold.

## Exceptions

Incidental text has no contrast requirement: text that is part of an inactive user interface component, that is pure decoration, that is not visible to anyone, or that is part of a picture that contains significant other visual content. Logotypes are also exempt: text that is part of a logo or brand name has no minimum contrast requirement.

## Intent

The intent is to provide enough contrast between text and its background so that it can be read by people with moderately low vision or impaired contrast perception, without needing contrast enhancing assistive technology. The 4.5:1 ratio was chosen to compensate for the loss in contrast sensitivity typical of users with roughly 20/40 vision, and 3:1 for large text because larger, wider strokes are easier to perceive at lower contrast.

title: Kara Pernice & Raluca Budiu, Nielsen Norman Group: Hamburger Menus and Hidden Navigation Hurt UX Metrics
text:
## Hidden navigation hurts UX metrics

Hiding the primary navigation behind a hamburger icon reduces discoverability and slows users down. In a study with 179 participants across 6 websites on both mobile and desktop, hidden navigation performed measurably worse than visible or combination navigation.

## Three navigation styles

Hidden navigation keeps the menu behind an icon such as a hamburger, revealed only on tap or click. Visible navigation shows the menu options directly in the interface. Combo (combination) navigation shows a few important options visibly while keeping the rest behind the icon.

## Quantitative findings

On desktop, users used hidden navigation in only 27% of cases, versus 48 to 50% for visible or combo navigation. Hidden navigation caused a more than 20% drop in content discoverability. Users rated tasks with hidden navigation about 21% more difficult, and desktop users were at least 39% slower with hidden navigation, while mobile users were about 15% slower.

## Recommendations

Do not use hidden navigation such as a hamburger icon in desktop interfaces where there is room to show options; display navigation at the top or side of the page. On mobile, where space is scarce, a hamburger or combo menu can be a reasonable compromise for 4 or more items, but the measurable penalty to discoverability and speed still applies, so keep the most important destinations visible when you can.

title: Kathryn Whitenton, Nielsen Norman Group: Website Forms Usability, Top 10 Recommendations
text:
## Website forms usability

Well designed forms lower effort and raise completion. The core recommendations are about layout, labels, length, and clear actions.

## Single column layout

Keep one field per row in a single column. Multiple columns interrupt the vertical momentum of moving down the form and force users to reorient their eyes, and they create ambiguity about the order in which fields should be completed. A single column preserves a clear top to bottom path.

## Labels

Place labels immediately next to or directly above their fields so the association is unambiguous, and prefer top aligned labels on mobile and shorter forms because they let users scan the form in a single downward glance. Avoid using placeholder text as the only label.

## Keep it short

Remove any field whose information can be derived, collected later, or omitted. Every time you cut a field or question from a form, you increase its conversion rate. Minimize optional fields, limit the form to only 1 or 2 optional fields, and clearly label them as optional rather than marking every required field.

## Grouping and actions

Visually group related fields into sections, and use grouping markup so screen readers convey the structure. Avoid Reset or Clear buttons, which risk wiping a user's work. Use a single prominent primary action, and give any secondary action such as Cancel much less visual weight so it is not clicked by accident.

title: web.dev (Google), Accessible tap targets
text:
## Accessible tap targets

Interactive elements such as buttons and links must be large enough and spaced enough to tap accurately on a touchscreen. When your design is displayed on a mobile device, make sure that interactive elements are large enough and have enough space around them.

## Minimum size and spacing

Use a minimum tap target size of 48 by 48 pixels on a mobile device with a properly configured viewport. This corresponds to about 9mm, roughly the size of a person's finger pad, which is the value Material Design recommends. Keep at least 8 pixels of spacing between tap targets, both horizontally and vertically, so users do not accidentally activate an adjacent element.

## Detecting touch

Rather than guessing device type, use media queries to detect touch capability. Test for the any-pointer: coarse media feature to increase padding for any touchscreen user regardless of device, since a coarse pointer indicates an imprecise input such as a finger. You can verify actual rendered sizes with the browser developer tools layout and computed panes.

title: Nick Babich, Smashing Magazine: The Role Of Empty States In User Onboarding
text:
## Empty states

An empty state is a screen that has no content yet and requires user action to populate it with data. A blank screen is not neutral: it is a critical moment where the app either guides the new user toward productive engagement or leaves them stranded.

## Three types of empty state

First use or first time state, shown when the user first opens the app or a section before any data exists. Success or user cleared state, shown after the user has completed or cleared all items, for example an empty inbox or a finished to do list. Error or no data state, shown when a search or action returns no results.

## The first-use state is an onboarding opportunity

Rather than presenting a blank screen, use the first use empty state to educate and engage. Show what the feature does and how to fill it, so the empty screen becomes part of onboarding and builds the user's confidence to take the first action.

## Key elements and best practices

Include a clear, scannable message that explains what the user can do, a supporting visual that conveys personality, and a prominent call to action that directs the next step. Avoid dead ends with no guidance, keep the layout visually simple, provide intuitive context and instructions, add personality and emotion, personalize the starter content where possible, and celebrate progress in the success state.

title: Vitaly Friedman, Smashing Magazine: Hidden vs. Disabled In UX
text:
## Hidden vs disabled

Both hiding and disabling features can be utterly confusing to users. A disabled control gives no explanation of why it is unavailable, no guidance on how to make it available, and often poor contrast that fails accessibility, while a hidden control simply cannot be found.

## When to disable, hide, or keep enabled

Disable a control when the user should know the feature exists but it is temporarily unavailable, for example an incompatible filter or a processing state. Hide a control only when the user will never have access to it, for example permission based or admin only features. Prefer keeping the control enabled as the default: let the user interact and then provide an inline explanation of what is missing.

## Key recommendation

Rather than removing unavailable options, explain why a feature is disabled and also how to re enable it. Preferring enabled buttons with contextual, inline error messaging over preventive disabling keeps the interface discoverable and teaches the user what to do, instead of leaving a dead, silent control on the screen.

## Anti-pattern to avoid

Disabling the primary submit button until a form is valid is a common anti pattern: the user cannot tell what is wrong or what remains, and gets no feedback on tapping it. Allow submission and surface clear, specific validation errors instead.

title: IBM Carbon Design System, Disabled states pattern
text:
## Disabled states

A disabled state is applied to a component when the user is not allowed to interact with it due to permissions, dependencies, or prerequisites. Disabling completely removes the interactive function of the component.

## Disabled vs read-only vs hidden

Default disabled cannot be clicked, selected, or interacted with, is not read by a screen reader, and takes on the default disabled visual style. Read only means the user cannot interact with the component but the content is still readable and accessible to a screen reader, and its styling must exclude interactive indicators. Hidden is used for permission based restrictions: the component stays completely invisible until access permissions change.

## Styling of a disabled component

Carbon specifies concrete visual treatments for the default disabled style: component opacity 50%, text opacity 25%, icon opacity 50%, no hover state, and a not-allowed cursor. Removing the hover response and changing the cursor signals clearly that the control is inert.

## Alternatives to disabling

Because a disabled control gives the user no explanation, prefer an alternative when you can. Use an inline warning or notification to describe how the user can re enable a disabled component, especially when disabling affects multiple items, so the user understands the prerequisite rather than facing a silent dead control.
